Snoqualmie

This starting path follows the Snoqualmie Indian Tribe’s own accounts of political recognition, language learning and advocacy around Snoqualmie Falls. The sources preserve distinct institutional, historical and cultural perspectives; they do not replace a fuller community history.

01

Identity and context

The Snoqualmie Indian Tribe has homelands in the Snoqualmie Valley and surrounding region.

Read the sources [1] Snoqualmie Indian Tribe

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Tribe-published history, language, land and contemporary institutions. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] Snoqualmie Indian Tribe [2] Snoqualmie Indian Tribe Culture Department [3] snoqualmietribe.us

03

Recognition and commemoration in the Tribe’s own account

The Tribe’s 2020 Rights Day retrospective distinguishes an initial recognition determination in 1997 from the later affirmation in 1999. It explains how an annual commemoration grew from that history. This is the Tribe’s institutional account; the linked federal records require separate reading.

Read the sources [4] Snoqualmie Indian Tribe, Governmental Affairs & Special Projects Department

04

Language learning through community resources

The Culture Department describes written materials and recordings as tools for renewing Lushootseed within the community. Its introduction connects earlier speakers’ work with present learning resources. The linked audio, stories and lessons should be approached through the department’s own instructions.

Read the sources [2] Snoqualmie Indian Tribe Culture Department

05

A public landscape and a history of advocacy

The Tribe’s account dates its Salish Lodge and adjacent-land purchase to 2019 and explains its significance after years of advocacy around Snoqualmie Falls. The dated landscape image introduces that named setting. It does not establish land ownership or reproduce the Tribe’s creation narratives.

Read the sources [5] Snoqualmie Indian Tribe, Governmental Affairs & Special Projects Department
